text.p: These are the leading stories in the Zimbabwe press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Zimbabwe's Supreme Court yesterday ordered information, posts and telecommunications minister Joyce Mujuru to grant black businessmen Strive Masiyiwa or any other applicant a licence to operate a cellular telephone network by the end of February next year.

- The government, facing a storm of protests from farmers, this week suddenly withdrew its plans to introduce sweeping levies on virtually all farm products, saying it needed more thime for consultations.

- Zimbabwe's Indigenous (black) Business Development Centre (IBDC), has urged the government to bar foreign and non-indegenous companies from acquiring mining rights unless they give at least 61 percent shareholding to local black companies.
- The loss-making Cold Storage Company, which is under-utilising its huge and expensive infrastructure, plans to off-load at least one of its abattoirs and reduce two others to seasonal ones.
- Most of the top managers at African Associated Mines, Zimbabwe's sole asbestos producer, are being retired in a shake-up designed to create a leaner and more focused management.

- A Dutch donor has come to the rescue of 43 former employees of liquidated firm Sayprint Textiles by injecting a soft loan of Z$1.3 million into a new screen printing company formed by the employees.
- The Zimbabwean government plans to intruduce a bill which will see civil servants enjoying the same benefits as those currently being enjoyed by workers in the private sector.

- Zimbabwe has been forced to increase power imports from Zambia and Zaire by 100 MW to a total of 250 MW with effect from January to boost supplies while a 420 kV inter-connector from Mozambique is being completed.

- Zimbabwe's Supreme Court on Wednesday ordered the minister of information, posts and telecommunications to expedite the outstanding administrative procedures on the licensing of cellular telecommunication services.
